title: Is Manchester United’s Bruno Fernandes the best player in the Premier League right now?
content:
Even someone as measured in his public comments as Michael Carrick came close to answering that question unequivocally after Manchester United’s fourth win in a row.

“Yeah, quite possibly,” he bellowed.

A No 10 who had scored his first goal in seven games, shinning the ball in at the far post past Tottenham Hotspur goalkeeper Guglielmo Vicario, would not normally enter such conversations. But that statistic, taken in isolation, overlooks everything Bruno Fernandes has brought to United since returning from a rare injury last month.

There was no assist for Fernandes in this 2-0 win over Tottenham Hotspur, but there had been six in his previous five appearances; five in four in the league, taking his tally up to 12 for the campaign, pulling Thierry Henry and Kevin De Bruyne’s Premier League record of 20 into view.

Dig one level deeper, and his creative numbers are in a different stratosphere than his peers. Fernandes has created 74 chances in the league this season — 27 more than the next best, Arsenal’s Declan Rice. Twenty-three of those 74 chances have come over the past five league games since his return from injury, post-Ruben Amorim’s dismissal.

Fernandes’ goal on Saturday brought up 200 goal contributions in 314 appearances for United. The 31-year-old has reached that milestone in fewer games than Paul Scholes, Ryan Giggs, David Beckham, and Cristiano Ronaldo. Only Wayne Rooney has reached it sooner during the Premier League era.

How is he suddenly elevating a good individual campaign into a great one? The simplest explanation is the most convincing: Carrick has had the inspired idea to play one of the best No 10s of his generation as a No 10.

No doubt, Fernandes is playing further up the pitch than he was under Amorim, and having a greater effect on United’s play at the business end as a result. His 46 touches in the final third against Tottenham were his second-highest tally of any Premier League game this season.

Except, it is not quite as simple as that, because he is not just playing as a No 10. As Carrick pointed out post-match, Fernandes’ goal came from him taking up space on the left wing, arriving late at the far post to connect with Diogo Dalot’s expertly weighted cross.

“He can play so many different positions,” Carrick said. “He’s just got the quality in the big moments, that composure, and can make the difference for us, and it’s nothing new.”

Amorim rated Fernandes as highly as Carrick, as highly as anybody in fact. The only complaint he would ever air about his captain was that he could go in search of the ball too often, popping up in different positions all over the pitch rather than being more disciplined and sticking to a defined role.

“Bruno wants all the freedom in the world,” Amorim said in September, the week after defeat in the Manchester derby. “Sometimes he likes to go further (forward), but he has a job to do, and the important thing is not Bruno playing well, it’s the team playing well and winning football games.”

Fernandes was playing deeper for a reason: to assist United’s build-up play, as well as assisting the front three.

Amorim was aware that playing Fernandes deeper was detrimental to United’s attack, but not playing him deeper was detrimental to United’s all-round play. It was a balance he could not strike. “We need more Brunos,” he would say. United only had one Bruno, though, and one never felt like enough in Amorim’s system.

Maybe the answer all along, then, was to have that one Fernandes not play in a double pivot or as a No 10, but to play everywhere; not giving him a job to do, but giving him the licence to do any job he sees fit.

It was interesting that when speaking on the pitch at full time, after being asked to explain what had changed under Carrick, the word ‘freedom’ sprang to Fernandes’ mind.

“Michael came in with the right idea of giving the players the freedom to take responsibility on the pitch, to make the decisions that were needed,” the United captain told TNT Sports.

That freedom has brought greater fluidity, flexibility, and — crucially — unpredictability to United’s play over the past few weeks, as well as bringing results. Fernandes, in particular, is playing better than at any other point this season. And when Fernandes plays well, United typically do, too.

Fernandes had more kind words for Carrick. “He remembers what I told him the last time he was manager,” he said to TNT, thinking back to Carrick’s time as an assistant to Ole Gunnar Solskjaer. “Michael could be a great manager and he’s just shown it.”

The appreciation is mutual. “He’s always in and around big moments,” Carrick said of Fernandes. “He’s got his fingerprints on it most of the time.”

Fernandes’ fingerprints are all over just about every fast, crisp and fluid passage of play that United string together at present. He is revelling in the freedom he has been granted. On form, there is no better player in the Premier League right now.
